# What the Heaps Offer, and the Way Out

*SN 22.26, the Assāda Sutta — set 4, Not-Self and Dependent Arising*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 4 min · 559 words</p>

[Skip to the translation](#translation){ .reader-skip-link }

## Before you read

Here the Buddha looks back to the time before his awakening and tells you
what he was asking.

He took each of the five *clung-to heaps* in turn (form, felt experience,
recognition, putting-together activities and knowing) and asked three
questions of it. What is its *gratification*: what real satisfaction does it
offer? What is its *danger*: what is wrong with leaning on it? And what is the
*escape* from it?

Notice the order. He does not start by calling the heaps worthless. Each one
really does give satisfaction and gladness, and the text says so first. The
danger is that each is impermanent and changing, and the escape is not getting
rid of the heaps but letting go of the desire and passion for them.

The last part is the claim itself: he says he did not call himself awakened
until he had seen all three sides of all five heaps as they really are.

## Translation

### The Setting

At Sāvatthī, the Buddha said:

"Bhikkhus, before my awakening, while I was still unawakened but intent on
awakening, this thought arose in me:

### The Question

'What is the gratification in form, what is the danger in it, and what is
the escape from it? What is the gratification in felt experience, what is the
danger in it, and what is the escape from it? What is the gratification in
recognition, what is the danger in it, and what is the escape from it? What is
the gratification in putting-together activities, what is the danger in them,
and what is the escape from them? What is the gratification in knowing, what
is the danger in it, and what is the escape from it?'

### The Answer

"Then this thought arose in me:

'The satisfaction and gladness that arise dependent on form: this is the
gratification in form. That form is impermanent, dissatisfactory, and subject
to change: this is the danger in form. The removal of desire and passion for
form, the abandoning of desire and passion for form: this is the escape from
form.

The satisfaction and gladness that arise dependent on felt experience: this is
the gratification in felt experience. That felt experience is impermanent,
dissatisfactory, and subject to change: this is the danger in felt
experience. The removal of desire and passion for felt experience, the
abandoning of desire and passion for felt experience: this is the escape from
felt experience.

The satisfaction and gladness that arise dependent on recognition: this is the
gratification in recognition. That recognition is impermanent,
dissatisfactory, and subject to change: this is the danger in recognition.
The removal of desire and passion for recognition, the abandoning of desire
and passion for recognition: this is the escape from recognition.

The satisfaction and gladness that arise dependent on putting-together
activities: this is the gratification in putting-together activities. That
putting-together activities are impermanent, dissatisfactory, and subject to
change: this is the danger in putting-together activities. The removal of
desire and passion for putting-together activities, the abandoning of desire
and passion for putting-together activities: this is the escape from
putting-together activities.

The satisfaction and gladness that arise dependent on knowing: this is the
gratification in knowing. That knowing is impermanent, dissatisfactory, and
subject to change: this is the danger in knowing. The removal of desire and
passion for knowing, the abandoning of desire and passion for knowing: this is
the escape from knowing.'

### The Buddha's Declaration

"As long as I did not directly know, as they really are, the gratification in
these five clung-to heaps as gratification, the danger in them as danger, and
the escape from them as escape, I did not claim unsurpassed full awakening in
the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its
samaṇas and brahmins, its rulers and its people.

But when I directly knew, as they really are, the gratification in these five
clung-to heaps as gratification, the danger in them as danger, and the escape
from them as escape, then I did claim unsurpassed full awakening in the world
with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its samaṇas and
brahmins, its rulers and its people.

Knowledge and seeing arose in me:

'My release is unshakeable.
This is the last birth.
Now there is no more renewed becoming.'"

The fifth discourse is finished.

<details class="reader-terms">
<summary>Words used in this translation (14)</summary>
<dl>
<dt><dfn>awakening</dfn></dt>
<dd>Coming fully awake to how things are. Sometimes translated &quot;enlightenment,&quot; a word this project avoids as needlessly mystical.</dd>
<dt><dfn>becoming</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;bhava&quot; -- the settling of experience into a way of being that feels like somebody being something. Often translated &quot;existence.&quot;</dd>
<dt><dfn>bhikkhus</dfn></dt>
<dd>Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha&#x27;s usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly &quot;friends&quot; in force.</dd>
<dt><dfn>birth</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;jāti&quot; -- being born, and the link that ageing and dying depend on in the dependent-arising sequence. In MN 141 the word appears once in its everyday sense instead, in a simile about a mother.</dd>
<dt><dfn>clung-to heaps</dfn></dt>
<dd>The five categories experience gets sorted into and then grasped as &quot;me&quot; or &quot;mine&quot; -- body, feeling, recognition, mental activity, and awareness. Not clinging to the categories themselves, but to the sense of ownership placed on top of them.</dd>
<dt><dfn>escape</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;nissaraṇa&quot; -- the genuine way out of whatever is under discussion, as opposed to the false escapes an untrained mind reaches for instead. In SN 36.6 the escape is from being stuck in a feeling; in Ud 8.3 it is from everything born, made and conditioned.</dd>
<dt><dfn>felt experience</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;vedanā&quot; (often translated &quot;feeling&quot;) -- the immediate pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral tone of an experience, prior to any story built on top of it.</dd>
<dt><dfn>form</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;rūpa&quot; -- the physical, material aspect of experience, one of the five heaps.</dd>
<dt><dfn>gladness</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;muditā&quot; (often translated &quot;sympathetic joy&quot;) -- being genuinely glad at someone else&#x27;s good fortune, cultivated as a practice rather than assumed to come naturally.</dd>
<dt><dfn>gratification</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;assāda&quot; -- the real satisfaction something offers, which is why it is held on to. The texts pair it with that thing&#x27;s danger and the escape from it, so that all three are seen together.</dd>
<dt><dfn>knowing</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;viññāṇa&quot; (often translated &quot;consciousness&quot;) -- bare awareness of an object through one of the senses or the mind.</dd>
<dt><dfn>putting-together activities</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;saṅkhārā&quot; (often translated &quot;mental formations&quot;) -- the mind&#x27;s constructing and assembling activity, one of the five heaps.</dd>
<dt><dfn>recognition</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;saññā&quot; (often translated &quot;perception&quot;) -- the mind&#x27;s act of identifying and labeling what it encounters.</dd>
<dt><dfn>world</dfn></dt>
<dd>A word whose scope shifts with the teaching. It can mean the lived world built through the senses and the mind, or the wider physical cosmos. The surrounding passage shows which sense is meant.</dd>
</dl>
